items.title: REGULATORY PERSPECTIVES ON RISK-BASED MONITORING IN CLINICAL TRIALS OF HIGH-RISK MEDICAL DEVICES IN INDIA: A REVIEW
items.abstract: Clinical investigations of high-risk medical devices generate essential evidence for regulatory decisions concerning implanted, life-supporting, and potentially harmful devices. Traditional monitoring approaches, characterized by frequent on-site visits and extensive source data verification (SDV), are resource-intensive and may provide limited additional value in detecting critical errors. Risk-based monitoring (RBM), supported by risk-based quality management (RBQM), focuses monitoring activities on processes and data essential for participant safety and trial reliability. International regulatory bodies, including the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH), US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), European Medicines Agency (EMA), and International Organization for Standardization (ISO), support risk-proportionate quality management. In India, clinical investigations are governed by the Medical Devices Rules, 2017, administered by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO); however, dedicated provisions for RBM remain limited. This review examines global and Indian regulatory approaches to RBM in Class C and D medical device investigations. It discusses key components, including risk assessment, key risk indicators, quality tolerance limits, centralized monitoring, and targeted source data review. Published evidence regarding effectiveness, costs, and operational benefits is evaluated alongside device-specific challenges, implementation barriers, and emerging technologies such as electronic data capture, artificial intelligence, wearable sensors, and decentralized clinical trials. Traditional and risk-based monitoring approaches are compared, and a roadmap for integrating RBM into India's regulatory framework is proposed. RBM represents a scientifically justified and regulatorily supportable approach for high-risk medical device investigations, provided that a device-specific, CDSCO-aligned framework ensures documented risk assessment, proportionate monitoring, participant protection, data integrity, and auditable oversight.

items.title: Reordering Engineering Knowledge: Employability, Programming-Centred Learning, Group Dynamics, and the Emergence of AI-Mediated Technical Competence
items.abstract: This research proposal outlines an exploratory study into how employability expectations and the growing integration of programming, computational tools, simulation environments, and generative artificial intelligence may be reshaping students’ understandings of engineering knowledge and technical competence. It proposes to examine how engineering students perceive the relationship between programming proficiency, theoretical understanding, practical experimentation, and discipline-specific skills, particularly as software-based work becomes increasingly prominent in education and professional practice. The proposal also considers how these changing perceptions may influence group dynamics, expectations of competence, divisions of responsibility, recognition of contributions, and experiences of perceived inequity or dissatisfaction in collaborative settings. Drawing on Expectation States Theory and perspectives on equity, the proposed study adopts an exploratory qualitative approach to investigate how students interpret and experience these changes in the meaning and valuation of engineering competence.

items.title: Research Seminar: Artificial Intelligence Challenges and Opportunities in Social Work
items.abstract: A significant milestone in the field of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly large language models (LLMs), was reached with the introduction of the ChatGPT system by OpenAI in late 2022. Subsequently, other advanced models like Anthropic’s Claude and Google’s Gemini were released, broadening the possibilities for meaningful human–machine conversations (Hu, 2023). These systems, utilizing advanced natural language processing technologies, exhibit remarkable capabilities in managing dialogue, grasping context, and generating high-quality content. Creative AI has rapidly become integrated into the organizational and practical aspects of social work, and GenAI is already widely utilized by professionals and students (Singer et al., 2023; Tulğan & Güre, 2024). The question confronting social work educators is no longer whether to involve AI, but rather how to do so effectively to prepare students for critical, ethical, and proficient practice. Addressing this issue entails more than merely incorporating AI content into existing courses. It necessitates a learning environment that transforms the student’s interaction with GenAI from that of a passive user to that of an informed professional, someone capable of assessing a GenAI tool based on the specific requirements of a practice scenario, recognizing its limitations, and making well-founded decisions on when and how to use it. Social work students also need to know how to create AI-based tools for everyday practice (Kapur et al., 2025; Reamer, 2023; Stone, 2023; Tulğan & Güre, 2024). These advancements call for adapting social work education and learning methodologies to the digital era while incorporating advanced LLMs into professional teaching and training processes (Kapur et al., 2025; Singer et al., 2023).

items.title: Responsive Digital Pedagogy and the Social Sustainability of Digital Education: A Relational and Ecological Framework
items.abstract: Digital transformation has intensified questions about the sustainability of educational systems, yet sustainable digital education is often discussed in terms of technological capacity, access, efficiency and scalability. This conceptual article develops a distinct conceptualisation of responsive digital pedagogy (RDP) for the social sustainability of digital education. Drawing on scholarship on social sustainability, digital education, relational pedagogy, student agency and sociotechnical educational infrastructures, and informed by peer-reviewed research on responsive and democratic pedagogies, the article distinguishes sustainable educational provision from sustainable educational experience. It proposes four interconnected dimensions: relational sustainability, concerning recognition and pedagogical response; temporal sustainability, concerning attention and differentiated rhythms; participatory sustainability, concerning agency, plurality and meaningful influence; and infrastructural sustainability, concerning the technological and institutional conditions that organise educational possibility. These dimensions are examined through tensions between efficiency and attention, visibility and meaningful participation, scalability and relational density, and predictability and pedagogical openness. Socially sustainable digital education is therefore defined as the capacity of a digitally mediated educational ecology to maintain over time the relational, temporal, participatory and infrastructural conditions through which meaningful educational participation remains possible. The framework is presented as an analytical proposition for further empirical refinement rather than as a validated measurement model.
